clue.text: Follow men's fashion

blocks.note: to tail someone is to follow them
OR, other ranks, is crossword shorthand for ordinary soldiers or men

explanation.surface: Advice to keep up with the latest menswear trends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fashion' looks like a noun completing 'men's fashion', but it is the verb that defines the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To tailor something is to make or shape it to measure, a synonym of the verb fashion.

clue.text: See you pocketing one crown

indicators.note: something pocketing an item holds it inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: ta-ra is an informal northern English goodbye, like 'see you'
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A farewell to someone slipping a crown into their pocket as they leave.
explanation.walkthrough: TA-RA is a casual British way of saying goodbye; I goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiara is a jewelled headpiece, a type of small crown worn by women.

clue.text: Poor say city turned criminal

indicators.note: turned round means the letters of the preceding word are read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: poor health is ill health, so poor = ill
e.g., for example, is what 'say' means in 'a fruit, say'
LA, Los Angeles, is the standard city abbreviation

explanation.surface: A poor city that has gone over to crime.
explanation.definitionFit: Criminal and illegal are adjective synonyms for something against the law.

clue.text: Sort of skin, say, that is covering square

indicators.note: a covering lies over and around something, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: the skin is an example of an organ of the body
i.e., the Latin abbreviation for 'that is'
S is an abbreviation for square, as in street names

explanation.surface: A question about classifying skin types, said to be covering a square area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort of skin' reads as 'kind of skin', but 'Sort' is the verb on its own; 'of skin, say' points to the organ.
explanation.definitionFit: To sort things is to arrange them in order, which is what organising means.

clue.text: I wasn't worried about Kipling poem being satirical

indicators.note: worried as in worried at or tugged about, so these letters are disturbed into a new order
about means surrounding, so the shuffled letters go round the poem's title

blocks.note: the letters of these two words, ready to be rearranged
'If—' is Rudyard Kipling's famous poem

explanation.surface: Someone protesting they never worried that a Kipling poem was meant as satire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'If—' is Kipling's best-known poem; the shuffled letters fall either side of it rather than all after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Jonathan Swift wrote Gulliver's Travels and A Modest Proposal, so Swiftian describes biting satire in his manner.

clue.text: Choristers were storming Elgar's home

indicators.note: storming suggests wild, tumultuous movement, so these letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: every letter of these two words is used

explanation.surface: A choir rushing into the house of composer Edward Elgar.
explanation.walkthrough: Worcestershire is an English county in the West Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: The composer Edward Elgar was born near Worcester and lived much of his life in that county.

clue.text: Wrap up without a fight

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top, backwards
without in its old sense of outside, so the turned word goes around the other piece

blocks.note: a scarf is a wrap for the neck
taken as written

explanation.surface: An instruction to finish a matter quickly without coming to blows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrap up' looks like a phrase meaning finish, and 'without a fight' like a single phrase; it splits as a reversed scarf around A.
explanation.definitionFit: A fracas is a noisy brawl or disturbance, a synonym for a fight.

clue.text: One shouldn't trade in booze, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly means as heard or said, so the answer matches the sound of the phrase

blocks.note: cider is an alcoholic drink, so 'in booze' can be 'in cider'

explanation.surface: A rule that nobody should deal in alcohol.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trade in booze' looks like one phrase; 'in' belongs to the wordplay. Insider trading means dealing shares on secret information.
explanation.definitionFit: Insider trading is illegal, so an insider, with privileged company knowledge, is someone who shouldn't trade in its shares.

clue.text: E.g. one from a third of miners getting classical inspiration right

blocks.note: NUM is the National Union of Mineworkers, the British miners' union
Erato is one of the Greek Muses, those sources of inspiration
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Something about a third of the miners finding inspiration in the classics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a third of miners' looks like a fraction of the workforce; the third is the fraction 1/3, and 'of miners' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: In the fraction one-third, the one is the top number, which is called the numerator.

clue.text: Overpowering crew wave in chorus

indicators.note: in places the first pieces inside the word that follows

blocks.note: a crew is a team working together
a roller is a long heavy wave
to chorus is to sing together

explanation.surface: A rowing crew giving a wave while singing together.
explanation.definitionFit: Steamrollering means crushing opposition by sheer force, which is a figurative sense of overpowering.

clue.text: Returned list of details with bit of fish - a snapper?

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the whole string of pieces is read backwards

blocks.note: a rota is a list of duties or assignments
the gill is a fish's breathing organ
taken as written

explanation.surface: A returned list noting fish parts, with a query about a snapper, which is itself a fish.
explanation.walkthrough: A snapper is also a fish, which makes 'bit of fish' feel like part of the definition; but the snapper here is a reptile. The question mark flags the definition by description.
explanation.definitionFit: An alligator snaps its powerful jaws shut, so it is fairly described as a snapper.

clue.text: Tea service and tea finally on the counter

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the word just before it
counter as in running counter, against the direction, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: Mass is a church service
the last letter of the second tea in the clue

explanation.surface: A tea set and some tea set out on a kitchen counter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tea service' reads as a tea set, but 'Tea' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Assam is a strong black tea named after the Indian state where it is grown.

clue.text: Element of legalese perhaps avoided by judge

indicators.note: if something is avoided by a person, that person is left out of it

blocks.note: legalese is an example of jargon, specialist language
J is the abbreviation for judge

explanation.surface: A judge steering clear of a bit of legal language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Element of legalese' reads as a component of it; 'Element' is the definition, and J is removed from the start.
explanation.definitionFit: Argon is a chemical element, a noble gas found in the air.

clue.text: A Greek lover suppressing vote for Macedonian

indicators.note: to suppress is to hold down, so one piece keeps the other confined within it

blocks.note: taken as written
Leander is the lover of Hero in Greek myth, who swam the Hellespont to her
a voter marks a ballot with a cross, X

explanation.surface: A Greek romantic silencing a vote for someone from Macedonia.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexander the Great, the conqueror, was king of Macedon, so the Macedonian is a famous example.

clue.text: I passed over sin with Romeo, to give an example

indicators.note: lying over something covers it, so this word sits around the next pieces

blocks.note: taken as written
someone who has passed away is the late so-and-so
lust is one of the seven deadly sins
Romeo is R in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A confession of having overlooked a sin with Romeo, offered as an example.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passed over' reads as ignored, but 'passed' means dead, as in 'the late king', and 'over' wraps that word round the sin and Romeo.
explanation.definitionFit: To illustrate a point is to clarify it by giving an example.

clue.text: Opening of Nolan movie

blocks.note: first meaning: a beginning or start
second meaning: Christopher Nolan's 2010 dream-heist film

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as the opening scene of a film, but the two halves are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: An inception is the establishment or start of something, and Inception is also the title of Christopher Nolan's film.

clue.text: European tribe almost destroyed

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
something destroyed is wrecked and broken up, so the remaining letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the whole word, before trimming

explanation.surface: A European tribe very nearly wiped out.
explanation.definitionFit: A Brit is a person from Britain, and so a European.

clue.text: 75% majority allowed to enter reports

definitions.note: plural, where the answer is a singular news report

indicators.note: 75% keeps three quarters of the word, so its last quarter is cut away

blocks.note: the bulk of something is most of it
let means allowed
to let in is to admit; in signals entry

explanation.surface: A three-quarters majority vote to let in news reports.
explanation.walkthrough: '75% majority' reads as a voting threshold; it means three of BULK's four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A bulletin is a short official news report or statement, so it is a kind of report.

blocks.note: C is the Roman numeral for 100
the number spelt out

explanation.surface: A simple subtraction sum: one hundred minus one makes ninety-nine.
explanation.walkthrough: The minus sign is only a hyphen joining the two pieces. A 99 is a British soft-serve ice cream with a chocolate flake, served in a cone.
explanation.definitionFit: A 99 is an ice cream served in a wafer cone, so the cone is what the 99 comes in.

clue.text: Mystery writer not starting with bonus puzzle

indicators.note: not starting means the first letter is left off

blocks.note: anon, anonymous, labels a writer whose identity is unknown
a plus is an extra benefit, a bonus

explanation.surface: A crime novelist who won't kick off without a bonus puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mystery writer' suggests a crime author; here it is someone whose name is a mystery.
explanation.definitionFit: To nonplus someone is to baffle or confuse them, so it is a verb synonym for puzzle.

clue.text: For example, Botham's ball sport dropping peripheral nonsense

indicators.note: dropping the peripheral letters means losing those at the outer edges

blocks.note: taken as written
rounders is a British bat-and-ball game, like a simple baseball
slang for nonsense; these two are the outer letters removed

explanation.surface: A cricketer's ball game shedding the silly stuff around its edges.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters lost from the ends of BALLROUNDERS are B and S, which together are slang for nonsense. Ian Botham was an English cricketer famous for batting and bowling.
explanation.definitionFit: An all-rounder excels at both batting and bowling, and Botham is the classic English example.

clue.text: Make harmless meal, not finished by expert

indicators.note: not finished means the word stops short, losing its last letter

blocks.note: a dish is a meal or course
an expert is able, skilled

explanation.surface: An expert left a meal unfinished but harmless.
explanation.definitionFit: To disable a weapon or device is to put it out of action, making it harmless.

clue.text: Mark lifted M&S confectionery, losing head

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifted means raised upwards, so the letters read from bottom to top
losing its head means the first letter is cut off

blocks.note: the two letters, M and S
fudge is a soft sweet

explanation.surface: A shoplifter takes sweets from Marks & Spencer, the British chain store.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lifted' suggests shoplifting from M&S (Marks & Spencer, a UK chain store); here it turns the letters over.
explanation.definitionFit: A smudge is a dirty smear, a type of mark.

clue.text: As shown by graph, no MP enhanced capital

indicators.note: as shown by means displayed within the following words, so the letters are on view in them

blocks.note: letters running from the end of graph through the start of enhanced

explanation.surface: A graph showing a city's improvement without any MP's help.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs from the P of graph to the H of enhanced.
explanation.definitionFit: Phnom Penh is the capital city of Cambodia.

clue.text: Look to capture animal - with this?

definitions.text: Look to capture animal - with this?

indicators.note: capturing something means holding it inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: lo is an old word meaning look
an ass is a donkey

explanation.surface: Someone eyeing a rope and planning to catch a beast with it.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: the question mark asks what you might catch an animal with.
explanation.definitionFit: A lasso is a looped rope thrown to catch cattle or horses, the tool for capturing an animal.

clue.text: Perhaps Indian flying ace breaking leg

indicators.note: flying suggests letters scattered through the air, landing in a new order
breaking into something means getting inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange
in cricket the leg side is also called the on side

explanation.surface: An Indian fighter pilot breaking a leg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Indian flying ace' reads as an airman; 'Perhaps Indian' is the definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: The Indian is one of the world's oceans, so an ocean is what Indian may name.

clue.text: Did lounge, lacking guts to work?

definitions.text: Did lounge, lacking guts to work?

indicators.note: lacking guts means the inner letters are removed, keeping just the ends
to work the letters is to manipulate them into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
only its outer letters survive

explanation.surface: Someone lazing about because they lacked the nerve to go to work.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the answer: lounging around rather than working.
explanation.definitionFit: To have idled is to have lounged about doing nothing, avoiding work.

clue.text: Pair protecting bishop with altar cross

indicators.note: protecting something means surrounding and shielding it, so one piece goes around another

blocks.note: II is the Roman numeral two, a pair
RR, Right Reverend, is the title of a bishop
the altar is also called the communion table

explanation.surface: Two people guarding a bishop at a cross-shaped altar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Altar cross' reads as a church crucifix; 'cross' is the adjective meaning annoyed.
explanation.definitionFit: Cross as an adjective means bad-tempered or annoyed, which irritable also describes.

clue.text: They're laid up?

blocks.note: surface reading: patients confined to bed, or eggs laid by a bird
setter's reading: laid up means stored away, as savings put aside for the future

explanation.walkthrough: 'Laid up' usually means ill in bed; the eggs suggestion plays on hens laying, while the real sense is money laid up in reserve.
explanation.definitionFit: Nest eggs are sums of money saved for the future, stored away or laid up.

clue.text: Journalist turned in two articles from a range

indicators.note: turned means facing the other way, so the word is read backwards
in places the turned word inside the pieces that follow

blocks.note: ED, editor, is the usual crossword journalist
two copies of the indefinite article an

explanation.surface: A reporter switched to writing two pieces about mountains.
explanation.definitionFit: Andean means of or from the Andes, the long mountain range of South America.
